# X-ray Detection of the Young Pulsar PSR J1357−6429

We report the first X-ray detection of the young pulsar PSR J1357−6429, characterized by a spin-down age of 7.3 kyr, using observations obtained with the XMM-Newton and Chandra satellites. This detection provides new insight into the high-energy emission properties of this relatively young neutron star.

## Spectral Analysis

The X-ray spectrum of PSR J1357−6429 is best described by a two-component model consisting of a power-law plus a blackbody component. The spectral fitting yields a photon index of Γ = 1.4 for the power-law component, indicative of non-thermal magnetospheric emission, along with a blackbody temperature of kT = 160 eV, consistent with thermal emission from a hot region on the neutron star surface, such as a polar cap.

## Luminosity and Energy Conversion Efficiency

Adopting an estimated distance of 2.5 kpc, we derive a 2–10 keV luminosity of approximately 1.2 × 10³² erg/s for PSR J1357−6429. When compared to the pulsar's spin-down power, this luminosity corresponds to one of the lowest known efficiencies for converting rotational kinetic energy into X-ray emission among the population of X-ray-detected pulsars. This result places PSR J1357−6429 in an interesting regime for studies of pulsar X-ray emission mechanisms and their dependence on age and spin-down power.

## Spatial Coincidence and Pulsar Wind Nebula Constraints

High-resolution Chandra observations confirm that the X-ray source is positionally coincident with the known radio counterpart of PSR J1357−6429, firmly establishing the identification of the X-ray emission with the pulsar. Furthermore, these observations allow us to place a stringent upper limit on the luminosity of any compact pulsar wind nebula (PWN) that might surround the pulsar, constraining it to be below 3 × 10³¹ erg/s in the 2–10 keV band. This limit suggests either the absence of a bright PWN or a nebula significantly fainter than those observed around other young pulsars with comparable spin-down luminosities.

## Search for Pulsed Emission

We conducted a search for pulsed X-ray emission at the known radio pulsation frequency of PSR J1357−6429, but no significant signal was detected. Based on this non-detection, we establish an upper limit of 30% on the pulsed fraction (modulation amplitude) of the X-ray emission. This constraint provides useful information for future theoretical modeling of the pulsar's emission geometry and the spatial distribution of X-ray-emitting regions on the neutron star surface.

## Summary

These combined results from XMM-Newton and Chandra observations establish PSR J1357−6429 as a young pulsar with unusually low X-ray efficiency, a spectrum dominated by both thermal and non-thermal components, and no evidence for either a compact pulsar wind nebula or strong pulsed emission within current sensitivity limits. Further multi-wavelength and deeper X-ray observations will be valuable for refining these constraints and better understanding the emission processes at work in this system.

# X-ray Observations of the Young Pulsar PSR J1357-6429: Detection, Spectral Characterization, and Search for Pulsations

## Abstract

We present the first X-ray detection of PSR J1357-6429, a young radio pulsar with characteristic age of ~7.3 kyr and spin-down luminosity of Ė ~3.1×10^36 erg/s, using archival XMM-Newton and Chandra observations. This pulsar had previously evaded detection in X-rays despite its youth and relatively high rotational energy loss rate, making it an important target for understanding the diversity of high-energy emission properties among young neutron stars. Our analysis reveals a point source positionally coincident with the radio pulsar timing position, with a spectrum well-described by an absorbed power-law plus blackbody model. The derived X-ray luminosity in the 2-10 keV band is unusually low (~1.2×10^32 erg/s), corresponding to an X-ray efficiency (Lx/Ė) of approximately 4×10^-5, placing this pulsar among the least X-ray efficient young pulsars known. We searched for pulsed emission at the known radio period but found no significant modulation, with an upper limit on the pulsed fraction of 30%. Similarly, no extended pulsar wind nebula emission was detected around the point source, with an upper limit on nebula luminosity of 3×10^31 erg/s in the 2-10 keV band. These results provide new observational constraints on the high-energy emission mechanisms of this enigmatic young pulsar and contribute to the broader understanding of the X-ray efficiency distribution among the young pulsar population.

## 1. Introduction

Rotation-powered pulsars represent excellent laboratories for studying the physics of neutron stars, their magnetospheres, and their interaction with the surrounding interstellar medium. Young pulsars, in particular, often exhibit multiwavelength emission spanning from radio to gamma-ray energies, providing crucial insights into particle acceleration mechanisms operating in extreme magnetic field environments. X-ray observations of young pulsars can reveal thermal emission from the cooling neutron star surface, non-thermal magnetospheric emission, and extended pulsar wind nebulae (PWNe) formed by the interaction of the relativistic pulsar wind with the ambient medium.

PSR J1357-6429 is a young, energetic radio pulsar discovered in radio surveys of the Galactic plane. With a characteristic age of τc ~7.3 kyr and a spin-down luminosity of Ė ~3.1×10^36 erg/s, this pulsar was expected to be a promising candidate for X-ray detection based on the well-established empirical correlation between spin-down power and X-ray luminosity observed across the young pulsar population. However, despite several previous observational campaigns, no X-ray counterpart had been unambiguously identified for this source, leaving open questions about its high-energy emission properties and its potential association with extended nebular structures.

The apparent non-detection of PSR J1357-6429 in previous X-ray studies presented an intriguing puzzle, as pulsars with comparable spin-down luminosities typically exhibit X-ray luminosities in the range of 10^32-10^34 erg/s. Understanding whether this pulsar represents a genuinely underluminous X-ray source, or whether previous non-detections were simply due to insufficient sensitivity, is important for constraining models of pulsar magnetospheric emission and thermal evolution. Additionally, the potential presence of a pulsar wind nebula around PSR J1357-6429 would provide valuable information about the pulsar's proper motion, the properties of the surrounding medium, and the efficiency of particle acceleration in the pulsar wind termination shock.

In this study, we present a comprehensive X-ray analysis combining archival observations from both the XMM-Newton and Chandra X-ray observatories, leveraging the complementary capabilities of these instruments to achieve robust source detection and characterization. XMM-Newton's large effective area provides sensitivity for spectral analysis, while Chandra's superior angular resolution allows for precise source localization and enables us to distinguish point-source emission from any extended nebular component.

## 2. Observations and Data Reduction

### 2.1 XMM-Newton Observations

We analyzed archival XMM-Newton observations of the field containing PSR J1357-6429, obtained with the European Photon Imaging Camera (EPIC) instruments, including both the pn and MOS detectors. The observations were conducted in full-frame mode with the medium filter to block optical/UV contamination while maximizing sensitivity to X-ray photons. Standard data reduction procedures were employed using the XMM-Newton Science Analysis System (SAS), including screening for background flares, filtering for good time intervals, and application of standard event selection criteria (PATTERN ≤ 4 for pn and PATTERN ≤ 12 for MOS detectors).

### 2.2 Chandra Observations

Complementary Chandra observations were obtained using the Advanced CCD Imaging Spectrometer (ACIS), providing superior spatial resolution critical for accurate source localization and morphological characterization. The Chandra data were processed using the Chandra Interactive Analysis of Observations (CIAO) software package, following standard procedures for event filtering, bad pixel removal, and exposure map generation. The sub-arcsecond angular resolution of Chandra proved essential for confirming the point-like nature of the detected source and for constraining any diffuse emission component associated with a potential pulsar wind nebula.

## 3. Data Analysis and Results

### 3.1 Source Detection and Localization

Careful examination of both the XMM-Newton and Chandra datasets revealed a faint X-ray point source positionally consistent with the radio timing position of PSR J1357-6429. This represents the first reported X-ray detection of this pulsar. The source position derived from the Chandra data, which benefits from superior astrometric accuracy, is consistent with the radio pulsar position within the combined uncertainties, confirming the identification of the X-ray source as the counterpart to PSR J1357-6429.

### 3.2 Spectral Analysis

We extracted source spectra from both the XMM-Newton and Chandra datasets using appropriate source and background regions, with background regions selected from source-free areas on the same detector chip to properly account for local background variations. The extracted spectra were grouped to ensure adequate counts per bin for chi-squared statistics, and spectral fitting was performed using standard X-ray spectral analysis software.

Given the low number of collected counts, we tested several spectral models commonly employed for young pulsar X-ray emission, including single power-law, single blackbody, and combined power-law plus blackbody models. The combined power-law plus blackbody model provided the best description of the data, consistent with the presence of both non-thermal magnetospheric emission and thermal emission from either the entire neutron star surface or a hot polar cap region.

The best-fit spectral parameters yield a photon index for the power-law component consistent with values typically observed in young pulsars, indicative of non-thermal magnetospheric emission. The blackbody component, when present, suggests a temperature and emitting region size broadly consistent with thermal emission from a compact region on the neutron star surface, potentially associated with a hot polar cap heated by backflowing magnetospheric particles.

The absorption column density derived from spectral fitting is consistent with the expected interstellar absorption along the line of sight to this pulsar, providing an independent check on the reliability of our spectral modeling and the association of the detected X-ray source with the pulsar.

### 3.3 X-ray Luminosity and Efficiency

Using the best-fit spectral model and adopting the known distance to PSR J1357-6429, we derive an absorbed flux that corresponds to a 2-10 keV X-ray luminosity of approximately 1.2×10^32 erg/s. This luminosity, combined with the pulsar's spin-down luminosity of Ė ~3.1×10^36 erg/s, yields an X-ray efficiency (defined as Lx/Ė) of approximately 4×10^-5.

This efficiency value is notably lower than the typical range observed for young pulsars of comparable spin-down power, which generally cluster around efficiencies of 10^-3 to 10^-4. The unusually low X-ray efficiency of PSR J1357-6429 places it among the least X-ray efficient young pulsars currently known, raising interesting questions about the physical mechanisms responsible for X-ray production in this source and potentially pointing to unusual magnetospheric geometry, magnetic field configuration, or evolutionary state.

### 3.4 Search for Pulsations

Given the availability of contemporaneous radio timing solutions for PSR J1357-6429, we conducted a search for X-ray pulsations at the known radio period using the collected photon events from both observatories. Standard timing analysis techniques were employed, including barycentric correction of photon arrival times and epoch folding at the radio ephemeris period.

No statistically significant pulsed signal was detected in either the XMM-Newton or Chandra datasets. Given the limited photon statistics available from this faint source, we place an upper limit on the pulsed fraction of approximately 30% (at a specified confidence level), assuming a sinusoidal pulse profile. This upper limit, while not particularly constraining given the low source counts, is consistent with the pulsed fractions observed in other young pulsars where thermal and non-thermal emission components with different pulse morphologies may combine to reduce the overall observed modulation.

### 3.5 Search for Pulsar Wind Nebula Emission

Leveraging the superior angular resolution of the Chandra observations, we conducted a careful search for extended emission surrounding the point source that might indicate the presence of a pulsar wind nebula. Such nebulae are commonly observed around young, energetic pulsars as a result of the interaction between the relativistic pulsar wind and the surrounding interstellar or supernova ejecta material.

No statistically significant extended emission was detected above the background level in the vicinity of PSR J1357-6429. We derive an upper limit on the 2-10 keV luminosity of any associated pulsar wind nebula of approximately 3×10^31 erg/s, assuming a nebula size consistent with those typically observed around pulsars of comparable age and spin-down luminosity. This non-detection may indicate either the intrinsic absence of significant nebular emission, an unfavorable viewing geometry, or that the nebula luminosity falls below our detection threshold given the sensitivity of the current observations.

## 4. Discussion

The detection of X-ray emission from PSR J1357-6429, while confirming the pulsar as an X-ray source, reveals several intriguing properties that distinguish it from the broader young pulsar population. The unusually low X-ray efficiency is particularly noteworthy, as it falls well below the typical range observed for pulsars with comparable spin-down luminosities and characteristic ages.

Several physical scenarios could potentially explain this low efficiency. # X-ray Astronomy: Pulsars and the XMM-Newton Observatory

## Introduction

The study of pulsars (PSR) has been revolutionized by space-based X-ray observatories, among which the **XMM-Newton** telescope stands as one of the most powerful instruments ever launched. Named in honor of Sir Isaac Newton, this European Space Agency mission has provided astronomers with unprecedented insights into the nature of these extraordinary stellar remnants.

## What Are Pulsars?

Pulsars, designated with the prefix **PSR** in astronomical catalogs, are highly magnetized, rotating neutron stars that emit beams of electromagnetic radiation from their magnetic poles. As these beams sweep across space like a lighthouse, they produce the characteristic periodic pulses that give pulsars their name. First discovered in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell Burnell, pulsars have since become invaluable cosmic laboratories for testing physics under extreme conditions—densities exceeding nuclear matter, magnetic fields billions of times stronger than Earth's, and rotation periods ranging from milliseconds to several seconds.

## The XMM-Newton Mission

Launched in December 1999, **XMM-Newton** (X-ray Multi-Mirror Mission) is equipped with three high-throughput X-ray telescopes, each containing 58 nested mirrors that focus X-rays onto sensitive detectors. This design gives XMM-Newton exceptional sensitivity for detecting faint X-ray sources, making it particularly well-suited for studying the thermal and non-thermal emission from pulsars.

The observatory's key scientific contributions to pulsar research include:

- **Thermal emission mapping**: XMM-Newton has enabled detailed studies of the surface temperature distributions on neutron stars, helping constrain equations of state for ultra-dense matter.

- **Timing studies**: Its European Photon Imaging Camera (EPIC) provides precise timing capabilities essential for studying pulsar rotation and glitches—sudden changes in spin rate.

- **Pulsar wind nebulae**: The telescope has captured detailed images of the nebulae created when relativistic particle winds from pulsars interact with surrounding interstellar material.

- **Magnetar studies**: XMM-Newton has been instrumental in characterizing magnetars, an extreme subclass of neutron stars with even more powerful magnetic fields than typical pulsars.

## Notable Discoveries

Among its many achievements, XMM-Newton has observed numerous individual PSR objects, providing spectral data that reveals information about neutron star cooling mechanisms, magnetic field configurations, and the physics of particle acceleration in extreme gravitational environments. The observatory has also helped identify new pulsars through X-ray emission before their radio counterparts were detected.

## Conclusion

The synergy between pulsar astrophysics and XMM-Newton's advanced capabilities exemplifies how sophisticated instrumentation continues to expand our understanding of the universe's most extreme objects. As XMM-Newton continues its mission beyond two decades in orbit, it remains a cornerstone tool for X-ray astronomy, contributing to our knowledge of these remarkable cosmic clocks and their role in fundamental physics.

# X-ray Observations of the Young Radio Pulsar PSR J1357–6429 with Chandra and XMM-Newton

## Abstract

We present a detailed X-ray spectral and timing analysis of PSR J1357–6429, a young (characteristic age τ_c ≈ 7.3 kyr) and energetic (spin-down luminosity Ė ≈ 3.1 × 10³⁶ erg s⁻¹) radio pulsar, using archival and newly acquired *Chandra* ACIS and *XMM-Newton* EPIC observations totaling ~120 ks of exposure. The pulsar is clearly detected as a point source coincident with the radio timing position, with a total of ~450 net counts collected across the combined dataset, sufficient for basic spectral characterization but not for high-significance timing analysis of pulsations. 

The X-ray spectrum is well described by an absorbed power-law plus blackbody model, with the non-thermal component (photon index Γ = 1.4 ± 0.3) contributing the majority of the 0.5–8 keV flux, alongside a thermal component with temperature kT = 0.17 ± 0.04 keV and emitting radius R_bb ≈ 0.5–1.5 km (for an assumed distance of 2.5 kpc), consistent with emission from a compact polar cap heated by backflowing magnetospheric particles. A single power-law or single blackbody model alone provides a significantly poorer fit, supporting the presence of both magnetospheric and thermal surface components. The absorbed flux in the 0.5–10 keV band corresponds to an X-ray efficiency of L_X/Ė ≈ 10⁻⁴, consistent with the trend observed for pulsars of comparable spin-down power.

We searched for coherent pulsations at the known radio period (P ≈ 166 ms) using the *XMM-Newton* EPIC-pn timing mode data, finding no statistically significant signal. We derive a 3σ upper limit on the pulsed fraction of ~45% in the 0.3–10 keV band, consistent with the modest photon statistics available and with pulsed fractions observed in other young pulsars where geometric alignment of the X-ray beam may suppress the observed modulation. Extended emission possibly associated with a compact pulsar wind nebula is marginally detected in the *Chandra* data, though deeper observations are required to confirm its morphology and spectral properties. These results add PSR J1357–6429 to the growing sample of young pulsars exhibiting a two-component X-ray spectrum, offering further constraints on polar cap heating models and magnetospheric particle acceleration in energetic rotation-powered pulsars.
